title: Song of the Grass-Roof Hermitage, Lines 13-18
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: Here is a summary of the main teaching in 5 sentences: The poem by Keizan asks "Will this hut perish or not?" and invites us to look beyond our attachment to specific outcomes and concepts, recognizing that true wisdom lies in understanding that Buddha nature is present regardless of impermanence. This understanding allows us to see through uncertainty and recognize the presence of the original master within ourselves. Joden Bob Rose suggests that by letting go of attachments to external directions or phenomena, we can find steadiness and stability in our daily practice. By embracing this approach, we can cultivate a sense of freedom and joy, and deepen our connection with the world around us. Ultimately, the poem invites us to explore the nature of reality and our place within it, challenging traditional notions of good and bad and revealing an all-encompassing yet empty quality of consciousness.
topics: A Shining Window Below the Green Pines

sentences.text: *Your spiritual nature cannot be separate from his.
How could your basic mind possibly not have common ground?

The existence of states of happiness and misery, superior and inferior conditions, depends solely on whether or not one has developed determination, whether or not one has met an enlightened teacher.*
And the capping verse from Keizan says this: *How can we see this story?
All at once he raises infinity.
Never has he clung to anything beyond him.* So I would urge you all, if you have a copy, to pick up Keizan's Denko Roku and check that out.

So tonight, I think we could say we have a vision or an image of a bodhisattva ourselves practicing, making this effortless effort that Shardu mentions in his lecture, having the determination to realize, to trust the teachings of no self and permanence and emptiness.
The lines tonight are interesting.
The last line of the verse we studied last was *Will this hut perish or not?* In the Chinese, it's the first line of this next verse.
*Will this hut perish or not?
Perishable or not, the original master is present, not dwelling south or north, east or west.
Firmly based on steadiness, it can't be surpassed, a shining window below the green pines.
Jade palaces or vermilion towers can't compare with it.*
So, line 13: *Will this hut perish or not?* It's interesting that in this line and the next line, the character for ruin is repeated twice.
As a reader of poetry, when someone repeats a word twice, it emphasizes it.
Here in two lines, this word ruin is used four times.
So clearly imperishability, ruin, decay is right on the mind of Shardu when he's laying this out.
But it raises the question for us: what does this mean?
What is perishing?
What is ruin?
What is decay?
What is the form, our body, that rots, that changes, is being ruined before our eyes?
Shardu's line, *what meets the eye*, is the way it comes to mind immediately.

And line 14 then: *Perishable or not, the original master is present.* An alternative translation from Mitchell says, *if you say my hut looks shabby, I'll answer that the one mind abides right where it is.* Whether it's rotten or not rotten doesn't really matter, because the speaker, the one who's in this hut, ourselves, we recognize that, I like the Bob Dylan song, everything is broken.
Everything is broken.
I was at a Dharma talk that Zoketsu gave at one point, where he was focusing on where we live in the world.
He made the point over and over again that even as something is new, it's already broken, because it enters the world of transition, it enters the world of impermanence.
But here what Shardu is raising is that the original master is present, both incorporating and in contrast to this impermanence.
The translation has the original master.
That character can also be read as the host, and we'll raise that issue later when we talk about the host and the guest line.
My colleague Mr.
Hanson has provided a little translation for this line that would be, alternatively, *the master has been here from the beginning*, or *the host was originally here.*
So even before the hut, before the idea of a hut, before our self-concept, before the concept of concept, the original host was here.
One name for the original master is our original being.
In the framework of the Mahayana teachings, Dharmakaya is used, one of the three bodies of the Buddha.
As I was getting prepared for this evening, I remembered that I had read this essay from early talks by Suzuki Roshi in this anthology called Wind Notes.

He presented a talk back in 1968 about the three forms of the Buddha, the Triyaka, in which he presents the Dharmakaya as the Dharma body of the Buddha, the perpetual potential fundamental undeveloped Buddha body, the original master.

Another commentator calls this one way of conceptualizing the un-conceptualizable Dharmakaya: big mind, unified existence that lies beyond all concepts, the all complete perfection in which animate forms as well as the moral order arise.
In our tradition, this is embodied in the first of the seven Buddhas before Shakyamuni Buddha, the Vairacchana Buddha, who's characterized as like the sun.
I think we'll pick that image up again when we talk about the shining window at the base of the pine trees.
Suzuki Roshi goes on to tie this original master to our practice of sitting.
He tells us:
*When we say just sit, it includes actually all of the activity, all the potential activity which we have.
We remain in an inactive state, but we have infinite potentiality.
In this sense, our practice includes everything.
When we sit, we're just sitting.

Each one of us is sitting and each one of us is the Dharmakaya Buddha, but even though we are sitting, we breathe, our heart is beating, so we are inactivity, which are the other two parts of the Trayaka, the Sambhogaya Buddha and the Nirmanakaya Buddha.
We understand reality in this way,* he tells us.

So, *not dwelling south or north, east or west.
Firmly based on steadiness, it can't be surpassed.* Let's take those couple of lines and investigate a little more deeply.
I like Ben's discussion that these directions don't exist as real entities.
They really are mental constructs that aren't separate from everything else.
They're empty of separate independent being.

When I read these lines, I thought of Robert Aitken's quotation from the Diamond Sutra that I mentioned a couple of times ago: *Bodhisattva dwells nowhere and brings forth that mind.* To me, this not dwelling in these directions brought that notion up immediately again.
And it turns out that Shardu's teacher Huineng, our sixth [unclear: "patriot"], actually wrote a commentary on the Diamond Sutra.

What he says, the way he translates one of the lines, is *if the mind dwells anywhere, this is an abode.* And he then comments, *if the mind dwells even in nirvana, this is not the abode of bodhisattvas.

Not dwelling in nirvana, not dwelling on phenomena, not dwelling anywhere at all, this is the abode of the bodhisattva.* Red Pine translates that line, *they should not give birth to a thought attached to a dharma, nor should they give birth to a thought attached to no dharma.
They should not give birth to a thought attached to anything.* So this notion of not dwelling north, south, east or west is really a fundamental notion of not being attached to phenomena.
But at the same time, the obligation, the commitment of a bodhisattva is to be engaged in those phenomena, to save all beings.

That segues to *firmly based on steadiness, it can't be surpassed.* Another way to translate that line, again my friend Paul helped me, is *just sitting here securely on a firm foundation, that's the best thing, that's the top thing.* And it's interesting that the character for steadiness in the Chinese is a roof with a cow underneath it, like a stable.
Just playing around with that, in English the word stable is obviously a structure for livestock, but it also means standing firm, upright.
So in both languages, somehow this notion of a protection for our animals, maybe this is where the ox herding stories live, protected from the rain, a different kind of hut.
There's something about a stable that gives us both stability and a vision of uprightness and protection.
And Ben goes on to say that when we sit, as apropos what Suzuki Roshi was saying a minute ago, we make a firm foundation, we make a stable, upright foundation.
In that we're merging our intention to practice with our intent on practicing with ease and not struggling to attain enlightenment.
Because again, not dwelling in north, south, east, west, it's also not to be attached to enlightenment itself, but to practice, to save all beings.
We're often reminded by Suzuki Roshi that sitting itself, our practice of sitting, is enlightenment.
It's not trying to get to enlightenment, that is enlightenment.

And we chant *an unsurpassed, penetrating, perfect Dharma, the incomparable Dharma, and beyond comprehension and understanding.* So the steadiness is both a steadiness of practice and a steadiness of emptiness at the same time.
Again, one of those paradoxes that seems to be the root of our practice.
